title: Why Go Distributed?
description: Understand why a single machine isn't enough — vertical scaling walls, horizontal scaling, the 8 fallacies of distributed computing, and network partitions.

segments.text: So far, we've been thinking about single machines. But at some point, one machine just isn't enough. Today, we'll explore why — and why distributing a system is both necessary and painful.

Vertical scaling means buying a bigger machine — more CPU cores, more RAM, faster disks. It's simple and it works. Up to a point. The biggest servers money can buy top out, and their cost curve goes exponential. Doubling performance might cost ten times more.

Horizontal scaling takes the opposite approach: instead of one giant machine, use many ordinary ones. Need more capacity? Add another server to the fleet. This is how Google, Netflix, and Amazon handle billions of requests.

But here's the catch: distributing a system adds enormous complexity. Things that were simple — like reading a variable — become distributed coordination problems. A function call becomes a network request that might fail, arrive late, or arrive twice.
In 1994, Peter Deutsch listed the eight fallacies of distributed computing — assumptions that developers make about networks that are wrong. Let me walk you through the ones that bite hardest.

Fallacy one: the network is reliable. It is not. Packets get dropped, cables get cut, switches reboot. Fallacy two: latency is zero. Every network hop adds milliseconds. A cross-continent request can take a hundred milliseconds — an eternity for a database query.
Fallacy three: bandwidth is infinite. Fallacy four: the network is secure. These fallacies aren't just academic — every production outage you've heard about traces back to violating one of them.
segments.thought_prompt: Your code calls a remote service and gets no response. Did the service crash, or is the network down? Can you even tell?

segments.text: That question leads us to network partitions. A partition happens when some nodes can communicate with each other but not with others. The system splits into isolated groups, each believing it's the real cluster.

During a partition, you face an impossible choice. Do you keep serving requests — risking inconsistent data across the split? Or do you refuse requests — sacrificing availability? This is the essence of the CAP theorem, which we'll cover in depth later.
Real talk: network partitions aren't hypothetical. AWS, Google Cloud, Azure — they all experience them. Your system must have a plan for when part of the network goes dark. Hope is not a strategy.
segments.thought_prompt: For an e-commerce cart, would you choose consistency or availability during a partition?

segments.text: So why distribute? Because one machine can't serve a billion users. But distribution introduces partial failures, network unreliability, and coordination headaches. The rest of this tier is about taming that complexity. Buckle up — it's going to be a fascinating ride.
